Chapter 3: Embracing Healthy Conflict for Better Decisions
Once your team’s built that foundation of trust, you’ll run into the next big challenge—learning how to engage in healthy conflict.
Now, I know the word “conflict” can make people uneasy. Most of us picture arguments, hurt feelings, maybe even chaos. But in a strong team, conflict doesn’t have to be about personal attacks or power struggles. Instead, it’s really about passionate debates, honest disagreements, and working together to discover the best ideas.
Here’s the thing—when there isn’t enough trust, teams tend to avoid conflict altogether. People hold back what they’re really thinking, nod along just to keep the peace, and steer clear of tough conversations. On the surface, it might look like everyone’s getting along, but underneath, issues start to simmer. And when problems aren’t addressed, they don’t just go away—they build up, leading to frustration, resentment, and some pretty poor decisions.
Picture this: you’re in a meeting, and the team’s discussing a new strategy. A few folks are worried, but they keep quiet—they don’t want to rock the boat or upset anyone. The group reaches a quick agreement, but really, the decision is built on shaky ground. Later on, when things go wrong, everyone’s left thinking, “Why didn’t I speak up?”
Healthy conflict is a whole different story. It’s rooted in mutual respect and a shared commitment to the team’s success. So, what does that look like in practice?
First, it means encouraging open debate. Everyone should feel safe to challenge ideas, question assumptions, and offer up new perspectives—even if they go against the grain.
Second, it’s about separating ideas from individuals. The disagreement is about the concept, not anyone’s personal worth.
And third, staying focused on the real issue. The goal isn’t to win an argument—it’s to find the best possible solution.
Now, if you’re leading a team, there are a few things you can do to make this kind of conflict possible. One—actively invite dissenting views. Reach out to quieter team members and make sure everyone’s voice is heard. Two—model calm disagreement yourself. Show that it’s totally fine to disagree, as long as it’s done with respect. And three—set ground rules for how to debate and give constructive feedback.
There are some practical tools you can try, too. For example, mining for conflict. That’s when you deliberately bring up hidden disagreements by asking probing questions. Or, you might give real-time permission—reminding the team, right in the moment, that conflict is not just okay, it’s actually encouraged and valued.
When teams embrace healthy conflict, the benefits are huge. You get more diverse viewpoints, you spot potential problems early, and everyone feels like they’ve had input in the outcome.
In the end, conflict becomes a tool for growth, not something that tears the team apart.
